analogy.p: A scalar is like being told 'the treasure is 50 paces away' (how far, but no way to find it). A vector is like 'the treasure is 50 paces north-east': you get both size and direction. This maps correctly because a vector needs both pieces of information to locate the answer. It breaks down because treasure directions are usually about position, whereas vectors in physics also describe things like forces that act on objects without any 'journey'.

bullets: A **physical quantity** is something that can be measured, and it is written as a **number (magnitude) plus a unit**, e.g. 12 m/s or 40 N.
A **scalar quantity** has **magnitude only** (size only), with no direction.
A **vector quantity** has **both magnitude and direction**.
The AQA specification wording is: 'Scalar quantities have magnitude only. Vector quantities have magnitude and an associated direction.' Use this wording in definitions.
Scalars combine by ordinary addition; vectors need direction to be considered, which is why forces are added as vectors to find a resultant force.

Knowing the type tells you whether a negative sign is possible: scalars like mass or time are not given a direction, while a vector's sign can show its direction along a line (e.g. +x to the right, -x to the left).
This idea underpins later topics: resultant forces, free body diagrams, momentum, and resolving forces into components (Higher tier).
core.h: What is a physical quantity, and why split them into scalars and vectors?
core.p: In physics we describe the world using **physical quantities** such as distance, time, force and velocity. Some are completely described by a number and a unit; others also need a direction before they make sense. AQA splits them into **scalar quantities** and **vector quantities**. The split matters because the two types combine in different ways: scalars simply add up, but vectors must take direction into account, so two vectors can partly or completely cancel. Almost every mechanics topic (speed and velocity, forces, momentum, acceleration) depends on knowing which type you are dealing with.

bullets: **Distance**: how far an object moves in total along its path, in metres (m). It only gets bigger as you move.
**Speed**: how fast an object is moving, regardless of direction, in metres per second (m/s). Speed = distance / time.
**Mass**: the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms (kg). It is the same everywhere.
**Time**: measured in seconds (s).
**Energy**: measured in joules (J). Energy stores have no direction.
**Temperature**: measured in degrees Celsius or kelvin.
Other scalars you meet in GCSE physics include **power**, **density**, **volume**, **pressure** and **work done**.
Scalars can never be negative as 'distance' or 'speed' (a speed of -5 m/s makes no sense), although a temperature below zero is possible because the scale itself has a zero point.
core.h: Scalar quantities: definition and the AQA list
core.p: A scalar is a quantity that is fully described by its size. If someone says 'the temperature is 20 degrees Celsius' there is nothing more to say about which way it points, because temperature does not point anywhere. The same is true for mass, time, distance, speed and energy. You are expected to recognise these quickly and be able to give examples. A good way to test whether something is a scalar is to ask 'does it make sense to say which way it points?'. If the answer is no, it is a scalar.

bullets: **Displacement**: the straight-line distance from the start point to the end point **in a stated direction**, in metres (m).
**Velocity**: speed in a given direction, in m/s. It is the rate of change of displacement.
**Acceleration**: rate of change of velocity, in m/s squared. Its direction matters (a negative acceleration means slowing down if velocity is positive).
**Force**: a push or a pull in a particular direction, in newtons (N).
**Weight**: the force of gravity on an object, in N, which always points **towards the centre of the Earth (downwards)**.
**Momentum**: mass x velocity, in kg m/s, with the direction of the velocity.
Other vectors you meet are **gravitational field strength** and **electric/magnetic field strength**.
Sign convention: choose one direction as positive (e.g. right or up) and the opposite direction as negative. State this clearly in calculations.
core.h: Vector quantities: definition and the AQA list
core.p: A vector is a quantity that needs a direction as well as a size to be fully described. 'A force of 10 N' is incomplete: pushing a door 10 N towards you has a very different effect from pushing it 10 N away. A complete vector statement is, for example, '10 N to the right' or 'a displacement of 5 m north'. The AQA specification names these examples: displacement, velocity, force, weight, momentum and acceleration. Recognise these as vectors by remembering that they all tell you which way something is happening or acting.

bullets: Distance is a **scalar**; displacement is a **vector**.
A runner completing one lap of a 400 m track has travelled a distance of 400 m but has a displacement of **0 m**, because the finish is the same as the start.
Walking 6 km north then 8 km east gives a distance of 14 km but a displacement of 10 km on a bearing of about 053 degrees (see worked example 1).
Displacement can never be larger than distance. They are equal only for straight-line motion in one direction.
On a straight line, displacement can be positive or negative depending on the chosen direction, e.g. +20 m (right) or -20 m (left).
In an exam, if a question asks for displacement and you give only a number, you lose a mark. Always add the direction (e.g. 'north', 'to the left', or a bearing).
Displacement-time graphs (a separate topic) have gradient = velocity, whereas distance-time graphs have gradient = speed.
core.p: This pair is the classic exam contrast. **Distance** is the total length of the path travelled, so it counts every metre walked and is always positive. **Displacement** is how far the object is from where it started, measured in a straight line from start to finish, **together with the direction**. Because displacement only cares about the start and finish points, an object that returns to its start has zero displacement however far it travelled. The two are equal in size only when the object moves in a straight line without changing direction.

bullets: Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector. Both have units of m/s.
A car travelling at 20 m/s north and another at 20 m/s south have the **same speed** but **different (opposite) velocities**.
Average speed = total distance / total time. Average velocity = total displacement / total time.
A change of velocity can be a change in speed, a change in direction, or both.
**Acceleration = change in velocity / time**, so anything that changes direction is accelerating even if its speed is constant.
For an object moving in a circle at constant speed the velocity is always along the **tangent** to the circle, so it changes continuously (see figure).
If a runner returns to the start after 100 s, the average speed is non-zero but the average velocity is 0 m/s because the displacement is zero.
Typical speeds the specification expects you to know: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s, car about 25 m/s, sound in air about 330 m/s.
core.p: **Speed** tells you how fast something is moving, whichever way it goes. **Velocity** tells you how fast and in which direction. Because velocity is a vector, an object moving at a constant speed can still have a changing velocity if it keeps changing direction. This is the key idea behind circular motion, which is why a car going round a roundabout at a steady 10 m/s is accelerating (its direction, and so its velocity, is changing). Two objects can have the same speed but different velocities if they move in different directions.

bullets: Arrow **length is proportional to magnitude**: a 4 N force is drawn twice as long as a 2 N force on the same scale.
Arrow **direction** shows the direction of the vector; the arrowhead marks which way it points.
Always state the **scale** when drawing to scale, e.g. '1 cm = 5 N'.
Label each arrow with its name and size, e.g. 'weight = 600 N'.
Arrows for opposite directions along the same line are drawn pointing opposite ways; equal-length opposite arrows cancel (balanced forces).
Vector arrows can be placed head to tail to add vectors: the resultant goes from the start of the first arrow to the end of the last (the **triangle method**, used in scale drawings).
Do not draw arrows through the object; draw them starting at the point where the force acts on the object.
A vector arrow is different from a ray arrow in optics or a flow arrow in an energy transfer diagram; each has its own meaning.
core.p: AQA states that a vector quantity may be represented by an **arrow**. The **length of the arrow shows the magnitude** (size) and the **direction of the arrow shows the direction** of the vector. To draw a vector accurately you need a **scale**, such as '1 cm represents 2 N'. Arrows are drawn from the point where the force acts, or from the object's centre of mass in a free body diagram. This visual way of showing vectors makes it easy to see when forces are balanced or unbalanced and to find the resultant graphically.

bullets: Same direction: 5 N right + 3 N right = **8 N right**.
Opposite directions: 5 N right + 3 N left = **2 N right** (take right as positive: +5 - 3 = +2).
Perpendicular: resultant = square root of (a squared + b squared). For example 3 N and 4 N at right angles give a resultant of 5 N.
Direction of a perpendicular resultant: angle = tan^-1 (opposite / adjacent). The angle must be stated relative to something (e.g. 'from north').
Scalars can simply be added: 3 kg + 4 kg = 7 kg, whatever the arrangement of objects. This is the contrast with vectors.
Displacements add as vectors: walking 3 m east then 4 m north gives a displacement of 5 m (not 7 m).
Distances add as scalars: the same walk is a distance of 7 m.
Higher tier: a single force can be **resolved** into two components at right angles to each other (covered in the resultant forces topic).
core.h: Adding vectors: collinear and perpendicular cases
core.p: Vectors add differently from scalars. When two vectors act along the same straight line, you add them if they point the same way and subtract them if they point opposite ways, then give the direction of the larger. When two vectors act at right angles to each other, the combined size is found with **Pythagoras' theorem** and the direction with trigonometry. This is how a resultant is found, and it links directly to resultant forces and free body diagrams. Higher tier questions may also ask you to find a resultant by drawing a scale diagram.

bullets: **Resultant force** is the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together; it is found by vector addition.
If the resultant force is zero the forces are **balanced**, and an object at rest stays at rest or one moving keeps a constant velocity (Newton's first law).
A force in the direction of motion speeds the object up; a force opposite to the motion slows it down; a force at an angle changes direction.
**Weight** (a force) always acts vertically down towards the centre of the Earth.
**Momentum = mass x velocity** (p = m v); the direction is that of the velocity. In a collision momentum is conserved, taking direction into account with +/- signs.
Gravitational field strength g is a vector pointing towards the centre of the planet.
Because the sign matters, always define a positive direction before substituting values into F = m a or p = m v.
core.h: Acceleration, momentum and force as vectors
core.p: The same vector thinking applies throughout mechanics. A force always has a direction, so when several forces act on an object we add them as vectors to find the **resultant force**. Acceleration is also a vector because velocity is: slowing down is an acceleration in the opposite direction to the motion. Momentum is a vector because it is mass times velocity, and mass is positive, so the momentum points the same way as the velocity. Recognising that these are vectors explains why direction signs appear in so many equations.

bullets: Constant speed + changing direction = **changing velocity** = **acceleration**.
The velocity at any point on a circle is along the **tangent**, at right angles to the radius.
For circular orbits, the force of gravity acts towards the centre of the orbit, changing the direction but not the speed of the satellite.
If the force towards the centre vanished, the object would move off in a straight line along the tangent (Newton's first law).
The Moon's orbit around the Earth: constant speed but direction continually changing, so velocity is changing.
A car turning a corner at 15 m/s is accelerating even though the speedometer reading does not change.
The SPEED stays the same but the VELOCITY does not: this single sentence earns marks in many exam questions.
core.h: Common contexts: motion in a circle, orbits and changing direction
core.p: The most important consequence of velocity being a vector is that moving in a circle at constant speed involves a changing velocity. Direction changes continuously, so the velocity changes continuously, and the object is accelerating. A resultant force is needed to cause this acceleration, directed towards the centre of the circle. Examples are a car going round a bend, a ball on a string, the Moon orbiting the Earth, and satellites in orbit. Making this link is a Higher-style answer and is regularly tested in 'explain why' questions.

bullets: A velocity of -4 m/s means 4 m/s in the direction **defined as negative** (e.g. to the left), so the speed is 4 m/s.
Speed is the **magnitude** of velocity. Always positive.
On a displacement-time graph, the **gradient = velocity**; a horizontal line means stationary; a negative slope means moving back towards the start.
On a distance-time graph, the gradient is speed and it can never be negative.
Velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration; area under graph = displacement (change in displacement).
If a question uses 'displacement', 'velocity', or 'direction' words it points to vectors; 'distance', 'speed', 'how far in total' points to scalars.
When a ball is thrown up and returns to the hand after 2 s, the displacement is zero but the distance is not.
Unit-based check: m/s could be speed or velocity, so the unit alone cannot tell you the type; the direction information does.
core.p: Exam questions often disguise the scalar/vector idea inside a context. You might be given a statement such as 'A cyclist has a velocity of -4 m/s' and be asked what the negative sign means, or a graph of displacement against time and asked to find velocity. Learn to translate statements into the scalar/vector language and to attach the correct type to each quantity. Remember that a negative sign on a vector indicates direction, not 'less than zero size'. On a graph, the gradient of displacement-time is velocity, so a negative gradient means moving in the negative direction.

bullets: **Free body diagrams** (4.5.1.3): arrows show every force acting on one object; arrow lengths show relative sizes.
**Resultant forces and Newton's second law**: F = m a is a vector equation; the acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.
**Momentum** (Physics Paper 2): total momentum before = total momentum after; use + and - for directions.
**Magnetic and electric fields**: field lines show direction (north to south for magnets), so field strength is a vector.
**Higher tier**: resolve a force into two perpendicular components, e.g. a force F at angle theta gives F cos(theta) and F sin(theta). Use Pythagoras and trigonometry to combine them.
Scale drawings: draw vectors head-to-tail using a ruler and protractor, then measure the resultant length and angle.
Typical combined question: 'A boat is driven east at 3 m/s in a river flowing north at 4 m/s. Find the resultant velocity.' (5 m/s on a bearing of about 037 degrees.)
core.h: Link to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Understanding vectors is the key that unlocks several other parts of the specification. In forces (4.5), free body diagrams show vector arrows for every force on an object, and the resultant is found by vector addition. In motion, displacement and velocity are used rather than distance and speed when direction matters. In momentum, conservation is applied with signs. In magnetism and electromagnetism, field direction and the force direction (Fleming's left hand rule) are vector ideas. In Higher tier, you must be able to resolve a force into components at right angles and to use scale drawings to find a resultant.

exam: **Definition marks (1-2 marks)**: 'A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.' Using both words 'magnitude' and 'direction' earns the mark.

**Give examples (2-3 marks)**: name a correct scalar (distance, speed, mass, time, energy) and a correct vector (displacement, velocity, force, weight, acceleration, momentum). Do not put them in the wrong group.
**'State the difference between speed and velocity' (2 marks)**: 'Speed is a scalar (magnitude only) whereas velocity is a vector (speed in a particular direction).'

**'Explain why velocity changes at constant speed' (2-3 marks)**: 'The direction of motion changes; velocity is a vector so a change of direction means a change of velocity; so there is acceleration.'
**Displacement calculations (3-4 marks)**: draw a right-angled triangle, use Pythagoras for the size, then use tan to find an angle and quote direction (e.g. bearing 053 degrees).
**Command words**: 'State' = short answer; 'Calculate' = show working and units; 'Explain' = give a reason using 'because'; 'Compare' = give similarities and differences.
**Drawing vectors**: use a ruler, label each arrow, quote the scale, and make sure arrow lengths are in proportion.
**Sign convention**: write 'taking right as positive' before using negative values; mark schemes reward clearly stated directions.
**Units**: write m for displacement, m/s for velocity, N for force. Marks are often lost for missing units.
**Graphs**: gradient of a displacement-time graph = velocity (give direction); gradient of a distance-time graph = speed. Mention the sign for vectors.
**Two-mark pattern**: one mark for the idea (vector/scalar), one for the application to the context (the actual object).

mistakes.r: Distance is the total path length (scalar). Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish in a stated direction (vector).
mistakes.w: Distance and displacement are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Speed is a scalar. Velocity is speed in a given direction. Same units (m/s) but different types.
mistakes.w: Speed and velocity are the same because they have the same units.

mistakes.r: The direction is changing, so velocity is changing and the car is accelerating.
mistakes.w: A car going round a roundabout at constant speed has constant velocity.

mistakes.r: A displacement needs a direction, e.g. '10 m north' or 'bearing 053 degrees'.
mistakes.w: Giving a displacement as just a number, e.g. '10 m'.

mistakes.r: Use Pythagoras for perpendicular vectors: resultant = 5 N.
mistakes.w: Adding vectors by simply adding the numbers: 3 N + 4 N at right angles = 7 N.

mistakes.r: Speed and distance are scalars and are never negative. A negative velocity or displacement simply shows the opposite direction.
mistakes.w: A negative speed or distance is possible.

mistakes.r: Mass is a scalar (kg); weight is a force (N) and a vector acting downwards.
mistakes.w: Mass and weight are both vectors.

mistakes.r: The displacement and average velocity are zero, but the distance and average speed are not zero.
mistakes.w: A runner who ends at the start has done no work or has no speed.

mistakes.r: Energy is a scalar. The transfer has a direction in the sense of from/to, but energy itself has magnitude only.
mistakes.w: Energy has a direction because it moves from one store to another.

summary: The specification asks you to know that scalar quantities have magnitude only whereas vector quantities have magnitude and an associated direction, to give examples of each, and to represent vectors using arrows. It matters because correct vector thinking is needed for displacement, velocity, forces, momentum and free body diagrams across the whole of Paper 2.

worked.ans: (a) distance = 14 km; (b) displacement = 10 km on a bearing of 053 degrees (53 degrees east of north).
worked.q: A hiker walks 6 km north and then 8 km east. Calculate (a) the total distance travelled and (b) the magnitude and direction of the displacement. (4 marks)
steps: Distance is a scalar, so add the lengths: 6 + 8 = 14 km.
The two legs are at right angles, so use Pythagoras: displacement squared = 6 squared + 8 squared = 36 + 64 = 100.
Direction: tan(angle from north) = opposite / adjacent = 8 / 6 = 1.333, so angle = tan^-1(1.333) = 53.1 degrees east of north (bearing 053 degrees).

worked.ans: Average speed = 5 m/s; average velocity = 0 m/s because her displacement is zero.
worked.q: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track in 80 s and finishes where she started. Calculate her average speed and average velocity. (3 marks)

worked.ans: The satellite's speed is constant but its direction keeps changing. Velocity is a vector (speed in a given direction), so its velocity is changing. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, therefore the satellite is accelerating, with the resultant force (gravity) acting towards the centre of the orbit.
worked.q: Explain why a satellite moving in a circular orbit at constant speed is accelerating. (3 marks)
steps: State that speed is constant but the direction of motion is continuously changing.
Link to vector: velocity is a vector, so a change in direction means a change in velocity.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so the satellite is accelerating (towards the centre of the orbit).
